meta.trial_name: CORONA (Controlled Rosuvastatin Multinational Trial in Heart Failure)
meta.drug: rosuvastatin 10 mg once daily (CRESTOR) vs placebo
meta.mechanism: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin); lowered LDL-C by 45.0% vs placebo at 3 months (about 1.6 mmol/L from a baseline of 3.54 mmol/L)
meta.indication: reduction of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI and nonfatal stroke in patients aged 60 or older with chronic symptomatic (NYHA II-IV) systolic heart failure of ischemic cause, not otherwise needing lipid-lowering therapy

n_randomized.quote: From September 15, 2003, to April 21, 2005, a total of 5459 patients entered the placebo run-in period, and 5011 patients underwent randomization at 371 sites in 19 European countries, Russia, and South Africa. Of those patients, 2514 were assigned to receive rosuvastatin and 2497 to receive placebo.
n_randomized.note: Registry S3 enrollment count 5013; design/baseline paper S4 (2005) reported n=5016. Intention-to-treat population defined as all patients who received a bottle of study drug.

median_followup.quote: The study was stopped, as planned, on the date that 1422 primary events were anticipated (May 20, 2007). The median follow-up time was 32.8 months. In total, 6290 patient-years accumulated in the rosuvastatin group and 6219 in the placebo group.
median_followup.note: 32.8 months = 2.73 years. The Discussion also refers to 'a median follow-up of 2.7 years'.

primary_endpoint.value: Time to first event of the composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke
primary_endpoint.quote: The primary outcome was the composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, and nonfatal stroke, analyzed according to the time to the first event.
primary_endpoint.note: Same primary endpoint in design paper S4 and registry S3. Deaths were 'classified as due to cardiovascular causes unless a definite noncardiovascular reason was identified', so sudden and pump-failure deaths count toward the primary endpoint.

inclusion_key_criteria.value: Age >=60; chronic NYHA II-IV heart failure of ischemic cause; ejection fraction <=40% (<=35% in NYHA II); investigator judged no need for cholesterol-lowering drug; no MI within 6 months; stable on optimal HF therapy
inclusion_key_criteria.quote: Patients who were at least 60 years of age and who had chronic New York Heart Association (NYHA) class II, III, or IV heart failure of ischemic cause (as reported by investigators) and an ejection fraction of no more than 40% (no more than 35% in patients in NYHA class II) were eligible, provided that the investigator thought they did not need treatment with a cholesterol-lowering drug.
inclusion_key_criteria.note: Mean age 73 years, 41% aged >=75 (S1 Results). Baseline paper S4: 'Mean age was 73 years (n=5016; 24% women), with 37% in NYHA II and 62% in NYHA III, ejection fraction 0.31, total cholesterol 5.2 mmol/L.'

planned_events.quote: To provide a statistical power of 90% to detect such a reduction in risk with a two-sided alpha of 0.05, 1422 patients with the primary outcome were needed. To achieve this result, we estimated that 4950 patients would be needed on the basis of a recruitment period of 16 months and a follow-up of 35 months.
planned_events.note: Observed 692 + 732 = 1424 patients with a primary event, i.e. the event target was met.

assumed_rrr.unit: fraction (mean overall reduction; 22% after an assumed 10-month lag)
assumed_rrr.quote: We anticipated that there would be a mean yearly hazard rate of 10.4% for the primary outcome in the placebo group. It was assumed that rosuvastatin would have no effect for 10 months but after that time would reduce the risk of the primary outcome by 22%, resulting in a mean overall reduction of 16.1% (i.e., to 8.7%), taking into account withdrawals from randomized treatment.
assumed_rrr.note: Assumed 16.1% overall reduction corresponds to HR about 0.84; the observed CI (0.83-1.02) only just includes it.

power.quote: To provide a statistical power of 90% to detect such a reduction in risk with a two-sided alpha of 0.05, 1422 patients with the primary outcome were needed.

alpha.quote: To provide a statistical power of 90% to detect such a reduction in risk with a two-sided alpha of 0.05, 1422 patients with the primary outcome were needed.
alpha.note: Three interim analyses (25%, 50%, 75% of events) 'with appropriate adjustment of the overall significance level'.

stopped_early.quote: The study was stopped, as planned, on the date that 1422 primary events were anticipated (May 20, 2007).

consensus_explanation.summary: Rosuvastatin cut LDL-C by 45% (about 1.6 mmol/L) and hsCRP by 37% versus placebo, but in 5,011 older patients with ischemic systolic heart failure the primary endpoint was not reduced (HR 0.92, 0.83-1.02, P=0.12; 1,424 events, matching the planned 1,422), nor was all-cause death (HR 0.95). The investigators and AstraZeneca attributed this to the population, not to LDL causality or the drug: nonfatal MI and stroke were uncommon, most primary events were cardiovascular deaths (mostly sudden), and those deaths came from a failing, scarred myocardium (electrical events, pump failure) that statins do not modify, in patients whose disease may have been 'too advanced to modify'. GISSI-HF found the same null result for rosuvastatin in heart failure of any cause, and the ESC 2016 heart-failure guideline concluded that statins do not improve prognosis in HFrEF and should not be started for HF alone. A pooled CORONA/GISSI-HF reanalysis that allowed for competing non-atherothrombotic deaths found fewer MIs with rosuvastatin in ischemic HF (HR 0.81, 0.66-0.99), so the atherosclerotic part of the mechanism still worked; this supports an endpoint dilution argument as a secondary explanation. Fewer cardiovascular and heart-failure hospitalizations and a post hoc benefit in patients with hsCRP >=2 mg/L were hypothesis-generating only.

sources.title: Rosuvastatin in Older Patients with Systolic Heart Failure
sources.note: Kjekshus J et al. for the CORONA Group, N Engl J Med 2007;357:2248-61 (issue 2007-11-29). Article text: 'This article (10.1056/NEJMoa0706201) was published at www.nejm.org on November 5, 2007.' Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion read from the Wayback capture; Tables 1-4 and Figures are images and were not read (Wayback image fetches failed). Key Discussion text: 'Nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke were relatively uncommon in this population, and death from cardiovascular causes accounted for the majority of primary events (and sudden death for the majority of deaths from cardiovascular causes). Rosuvastatin had no effect on the rates of death from cardiovascular causes or sudden death.' and 'In heart failure, sudden death may be caused by a primary electrical event that is related to ventricular dilatation and scarring.' and 'Since these patients may have had atherosclerotic or myocardial disease that was too advanced to modify, rosuvastatin might have had a different effect in patients with milder heart failure.' Also: 'Another possibility is that we did not follow patients long enough to see a beneficial effect of treatment.'

sources.note: AstraZeneca global press release dated '5 November 2007'; 'New data from the CORONA study presented today at the American Heart Association 2007 Scientific Sessions in Orlando, US'. Read from Wayback snapshot https://web.archive.org/web/20071109072458/http://www.astrazeneca.com:80/pressrelease/5357.aspx (web.archive.org/web/20071105/<url> resolves to this 2007-11-09 capture, the earliest; HTTP 200, full text readable). Live URL returns 403. The AstraZeneca homepage capture of 2007-11-08 lists it as '5 November 2007 : New Data Examines The Effect Of Adding A Statin...'; the previous release (1 November 2007) was the Q3 results. Topline: 'Patients taking AstraZeneca’s CRESTOR™ (rosuvastatin) 10mg experienced an 8 percent reduction (p=0.12) in the combined primary endpoint of cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction or stroke, which was not statistically significant.' Company/investigator view: 'In this study the majority of deaths were due to sudden death, or non-ischemic causes, which did not appear to be impacted by statin therapy.' and Kjekshus: 'Our findings suggest the major cause of death in these patients was likely not to be related to atherosclerotic events, where benefit with statins in non-heart failure patients has been demonstrated, but instead may have been caused by the deterioration of failing heart muscle damaged beyond repair.'

open_questions: Category: population (primary), design_or_endpoint (secondary). The investigators (S1 Discussion), AstraZeneca and the lead investigator (S2) blamed the patients' disease: deaths, mostly sudden, came from a failing, scarred myocardium that LDL lowering does not modify, and the disease may have been 'too advanced to modify'. GISSI-HF (S5) and the ESC 2016 guideline (S7) agree that statins do not improve prognosis in HF. The pooled reanalysis (S6) found fewer MIs (HR 0.81) and framed the null result partly as dilution by competing non-atherothrombotic deaths, which is the secondary endpoint argument. effect_too_small does not fit well: LDL-C fell 1.6 mmol/L, the 1,422-event target was met, and the CTT-predicted effect (~0.68) is far outside the CI (0.83-1.02); but the trial's own assumed 16.1% reduction (HR ~0.84) is just inside the CI.

Component counts of the primary endpoint (CV death, sudden death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) are in S1 Table 2 (image) and were NOT read; the Wayback image fetches failed. A secondary search snippet reported 227 vs 264 fatal and nonfatal MI and stroke events in a post hoc analysis; not verified, not used.

Absolute LDL-C change (-1.63 mmol/L) is derived from per-arm 3-month values; the time-averaged difference over follow-up was not reported in the text read. Open-label statins: 69 rosuvastatin vs 120 placebo patients.
